args.body:
DEVIATION REPORT
Analyze Counterparty Markup of Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement
Data Privacy & Cybersecurity

PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT

Prepared for: Client Engagement Team
Re: Counterparty Markup of Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement — Deviation Analysis

---

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

We have compared the counterparty's latest markup of the Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement against our original draft, firm playbook positions, and the operative disclosure schedules, and we have reconciled every deviation against the controlling partner instructions and transfer impact summary. The counterparty accepted most firm-standard provisions but introduced three material deviations:

1. Silent reduction of the indemnification cap coupled with conversion of the indemnification basket from a deductible to a tipping basket.
2. Addition of carve-outs to the definition of Material Adverse Effect (MAE) for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter.
3. A new, shortened limitation period that reduces survival for the core representations.

Consistent with the controlling partner instruction (the latest message in the deal team thread, which supersedes earlier contradictory messages), we recommend that the client CONCEDE the basket conversion (deviation 1, basket element) but treat the survival-period reduction (deviation 3) as a walk-away issue. Each deviation is analyzed below against the base materials, including the disclosure schedules.

---

II. DEVIATION 1 — INDEMNIFICATION: CAP REDUCTION AND BASKET CONVERSION

A. The Deviation

The counterparty markup silently reduces the indemnification cap and converts the indemnification basket from a deductible to a tipping basket. Under our original draft and firm playbook, the indemnification cap was set at the agreed firm-standard amount and the basket operated as a deductible, meaning the indemnified party bore all losses until the basket threshold was reached, after which only losses above the threshold were recoverable. The markup reverses this structure by making the basket a "tipping" or "threshold" basket, under which, once the aggregate losses exceed the basket amount, the indemnified party recovers losses from the FIRST dollar (i.e., all losses below the threshold become payable as well).

B. Reconciliation Against the Base Materials and Transfer Impact

Our original draft adopted the deductible basket as the firm-standard position, protecting the client from the incremental exposure that a tipping basket would create. The transfer impact summary, as reflected through Schedule 5.2, lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift. Specifically, the scheduled retained liabilities include matters that were carved out of the indemnity under the original draft on the assumption that they stayed outside the indemnity baseline. A reduced cap combined with a tipping basket changes the economics of those retained liabilities in two ways:

(i) a lower cap limits total recovery available to the client for breaches of representations and warranties; and

(ii) a tipping basket expands the recoverable universe to include first-dollar losses, increasing the client's realistic recovery by exposing the counterparty to the full quantum of covered losses once the threshold is crossed.

Because Schedule 5.2's retained liabilities intersect the indemnification structure, the cap reduction and basket conversion together would move a meaningful portion of those retained liabilities into the recoverable indemnity pool — a silent shift adverse to the counterparty and favorable to the client, but one that was not negotiated.

C. Analysis and Recommendation

Notwithstanding the adverse economics of the cap reduction, the basket conversion itself is treated as a concession per the controlling partner instruction. The client will concede the conversion of the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket. However, the silent reduction of the indemnification cap is a separate and independent deviation that must be addressed.

Recommendation: Concede the basket conversion as directed by the partner. REJECT the cap reduction unless the counterparty restores the cap to the original firm-standard amount. The cap reduction is not within the scope of the conceded basket point and would materially erode the client's indemnity protection, particularly given the Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities that intersect the indemnification regime.

---

III. DEVIATION 2 — MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT DEFINITION: REGULATORY ACTION CARVE-OUTS

A. The Deviation

The counterparty markup adds carve-outs to the definition of Material Adverse Effect (MAE) for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter. As drafted by the counterparty, the MAE definition would exclude from the meaning of "Material Adverse Effect" any change, effect, event, or development arising from regulatory action, investigation, or inquiry in the data privacy and cybersecurity space — the precise regulatory domain in which this cross-border data transfer matter operates.

B. Reconciliation Against the Base Materials and Transfer Impact

Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect the markup's MAE carve-outs. These inquiries concern the client's cross-border data transfer practices and data handling procedures. Under our original draft, a Material Adverse Effect would be available to the client if the outcome of these inquiries materially impaired the business, financial condition, or results of operations.

The counterparty's carve-out would exclude regulatory action arising from precisely these pending inquiries from the definition of MAE. This would disable the client's ability to invoke an MAE condition or termination right based on the adverse outcome of the disclosed regulatory inquiries. Since the disclosed inquiries are already pending, the carve-out is not a general or hypothetical protection — it is drafted to neutralize exactly the regulatory risk that Schedule 3.7 already flags.

C. Analysis and Recommendation

Because Schedule 3.7 discloses the two pending regulatory inquiries, and because those inquiries are "of exactly the kind at issue in this matter," the carve-out is a targeted attempt to preclude the client from relying on regulatory developments as an MAE. The carve-out is materially broader than any standard carve-out for changes in law or regulation, and it squarely implicates the subject-matter risk most central to this cross-border data transfer transaction.

Recommendation: REJECT the MAE carve-outs as drafted. If the counterparty insists on a regulatory carve-out, we should (a) narrow it to exclude matters not disclosed on Schedule 3.7, (b) add a "disproportionate effect" qualifier so that a carve-out does not apply where the effect falls disproportionately on the target relative to similarly situated companies, and (c) confirm that any carve-out does not extend to the specific pending inquiries identified on Schedule 3.7. The carve-out as drafted is not acceptable.

---

IV. DEVIATION 3 — SHORTENED LIMITATION PERIOD / SURVIVAL OF CORE REPRESENTATIONS

A. The Deviation

The counterparty markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens survival for the core representations. Under our original draft and firm playbook, the core representations — including representations relating to data privacy, cybersecurity, regulatory compliance, and other fundamental matters — survived the closing for the full firm-standard period, consistent with the survival matrix set forth in Exhibit B. The counterparty's markup shortens that survival period, reducing the window during which the client may bring claims for breach of those core representations.

B. Reconciliation Against the Base Materials and Transfer Impact

Exhibit B sets the survival matrix that the markup's limitation-period change contradicts. Under Exhibit B, the core data privacy, cybersecurity, and compliance representations survive for the full period, while non-core representations survive for a shorter, negotiated period. The counterparty's markup collapses this distinction by applying the shorter limitation period to the core representations as well, effectively rewriting the survival matrix established in Exhibit B.

The shortened survival period has direct consequences for the transfer impact. The disclosed regulatory inquiries on Schedule 3.7 and the retained liabilities on Schedule 5.2 would, in many cases, take time to develop into actionable claims. A shortened survival period could time-bar the client's ability to bring claims for breaches that emerge after the shortened survival window closes, particularly in connection with the pending regulatory inquiries whose resolutions may extend well beyond the shortened period.

C. Analysis and Recommendation

This is the deviation that the partner has identified as a WALK-AWAY issue. Under the controlling partner instruction (the latest message, which supersedes any earlier contradictory ordering), any survival-period reduction is treated as a walk-away issue. We therefore do not recommend conceding this point. The survival period for the core representations must remain at the full firm-standard period as reflected in Exhibit B.

Recommendation: REJECT the shortened limitation period for the core representations. Treat the counterparty's insistence on a reduced survival period for core representations as a walk-away issue. The survival matrix in Exhibit B must be preserved in its entirety for the core representations. No concession should be made on this point.

---

V. TRANSFER IMPACT SUMMARY

The transfer impact summary, as reflected in the disclosure schedules and corresponding analysis, supports the following conclusions:

1. Schedule 3.7 — Pending Regulatory Inquiries: The two disclosed regulatory inquiries directly intersect the MAE carve-outs proposed by the counterparty. Because these inquiries are disclosed and pending, they represent the primary regulatory exposure in this transaction. Any MAE carve-out that neutralizes the impact of these inquiries would strip the client of a critical protective mechanism.

2. Schedule 5.2 — Retained Liabilities: The retained liabilities listed on Schedule 5.2 are significantly affected by the indemnification changes. The reduced cap and basket conversion would silently shift the allocation of these liabilities, altering the negotiated risk allocation without explicit acknowledgment.

3. Exhibit B — Survival Matrix: The survival matrix set forth in Exhibit B is contradicted by the counterparty's shortened limitation period for core representations. The survival terms are central to the client's post-closing recourse and cannot be revised without materially changing the deal's risk profile.

Net transfer impact: The counterparty's markup, if accepted in full, would (i) expand the client's potential recovery via the tipping basket but simultaneously reduce the aggregate cap, (ii) neutralize the client's MAE protection for the exact regulatory risk most central to the transaction, and (iii) compress the post-closing window for claiming breaches of core data privacy and cybersecurity representations.

---

VI. SUMMARY OF DEVIATIONS AND RECOMMENDED COURSE

| # | Deviation | Counterparty Position | Recommendation | Priority |
|---|-----------|----------------------|----------------|----------|
| 1a | Indemnification cap reduced | Silent reduction | REJECT — restore cap to firm-standard | High |
| 1b | Basket converted from deductible to tipping | Altered structure | CONCEDE per partner instruction | — |
| 2 | MAE carve-outs for regulatory action | Added carve-outs for disclosed inquiries | REJECT — narrow to exclude Schedule 3.7 inquiries | High |
| 3 | Shortened limitation period / reduced survival for core reps | Shortened survival | WALK-AWAY — do not concede | Critical |

---

VII. CONCLUSION

The counterparty's markup introduces three material deviations from our original draft and firm playbook. Per the controlling partner instructions, the client will concede the basket conversion. However, the silent cap reduction, the targeted MAE carve-outs, and the shortened survival period for core representations must all be rejected. The survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue and should be treated as such in any negotiation.

We recommend that the engagement team (i) formally reject the cap reduction and require restoration to the firm-standard amount, (ii) reject the MAE carve-outs as drafted and negotiate narrowing language that protects the Schedule 3.7 regulatory inquiries, and (iii) reject any shortening of the survival period for core representations, treating it as a walk-away issue per partner direction. If the counterparty will not retreat on the survival-period reduction, the deal team should be prepared to walk away rather than accept the compressed post-closing recourse.

---

Prepared by: Deal Team
Law Firm Company
Data Privacy & Cybersecurity Practice
